title: A Wardrobe for the Aftermath
premise: Emrys Reyes, once the conservatory's most celebrated piano prodigy, returns a decade later as its night janitor, hiding in plain sight from the family that broke her. When her estranged grandmother dies, a stranger named Wren appears at the funeral calling the family by an old, secret surname — and reveals she holds letters Emrys's grandmother wrote but never sent, all circling one unfinished sentence about who Emrys really is and why she was sent away. As Emrys and Wren piece together the family's buried history — a hidden adoption, a silenced sibling, a name traded for respectability — Emrys must finally speak the sentence aloud to her dying father before the last person who could confirm it is gone. The novel ends with Emrys signing her recital program with both names for the first time, playing not as a prodigy or a penitent, but as herself.
about_author: Sable Ashgrove is the pen name of a former conservatory librarian who spent years cataloguing other people's dedications before writing her own. She lives near a defunct music hall and writes at night, when the acoustics are honest.

chapters.title: The Night Shift Sonata
chapters.summary: POV: Emrys. Three years into mopping the conservatory's floors after midnight, Emrys practices 'almost saying it' — rehearsing confessions to empty practice rooms she once filled with applause. A student recognizes her hands on the mop handle and asks if she's related to 'the prodigy.' Emotional beat: the ache of being unseen in the place you were most seen.

chapters.title: Black Clothes, Borrowed Name
chapters.summary: POV: Emrys. At her grandmother's funeral, Emrys stands at the edge of the family plot, uninvited by custom though not by law. Her father greets her like a colleague. Then a woman in an ill-fitting black coat says the old surname — Vael — and every head turns. Emotional beat: the vertigo of a word unlocking a locked room.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: POV: Wren. The stranger introduces herself: a archivist who found a box of unsent letters while digitizing a closed estate office, addressed to 'the Vael girl' — Emrys. She has spent months finding the addressee. Emrys refuses the letters, then steals one from the box when Wren isn't looking. Emotional beat: curiosity outpacing fear.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Never Mailed
chapters.summary: POV: Emrys. Alone, Emrys reads the stolen letter: her grandmother writing to a daughter given up decades ago, apologizing for trading the family name for a mortgage and a reputation. The letter ends mid-sentence — the same sentence Emrys has been almost saying for three years. Emotional beat: recognition, and terror of finishing what was started.

chapters.title: The Conservatory Remembers
chapters.summary: POV: Emrys. Emrys searches the conservatory archives during her shift and finds her own expulsion record sealed by her father's signature — dated three days after a recital she doesn't remember. Wren arrives with more letters; they form an uneasy alliance over bad coffee. Emotional beat: two strangers building trust out of shared paper.

chapters.title: Father, Interrupted
chapters.summary: POV: Emrys. Emrys confronts her father at his home; he deflects with anecdotes about her childhood brilliance. When she says 'Vael' aloud, he goes white and orders her out — but not before she notices the diagnosis paperwork on his table. He is dying, and he knows it. Emotional beat: anger colliding with a closing window.

chapters.title: The Missing Middle Sister
chapters.summary: POV: Wren. Wren traces the letters' intended recipient through parish records and finds a woman living two towns away — Aunt Odile, alive, unmentioned, erased. Wren visits her alone and hears the family's version: Emrys wasn't expelled for failure, but for asking about Odile at the wrong dinner. Emotional beat: the cost of silence measured in whole human lives.

chapters.title: Duet for One Survivor
chapters.summary: POV: Emrys. Emrys meets Odile, who plays her a fragment of their grandmother's composition — the piece Emrys performed the night everything shattered, taught to her without attribution. The two women reconcile the versions of the story between them. Emotional beat: grief becoming kinship; inheritance redefined as memory rather than property.

chapters.title: The Sentence
chapters.summary: POV: Emrys. At her father's hospice bedside, Emrys finally speaks the untranslatable sentence — 'You didn't lose a daughter, you sold one, and I am what you bought instead' — and stays to hear his broken half-answer. He gives her the original deed bearing the Vael name. Emotional beat: catharsis without absolution; truth spoken too late and exactly in time.

chapters.title: A Wardrobe for the Aftermath
chapters.summary: POV: Emrys. Months later, the conservatory hosts a memorial recital. Emrys takes the stage not as janitor or prodigy, prints 'E. Reyes Vael' on the program, and plays her grandmother's piece complete. Wren watches from the back row. Emotional beat: belonging claimed, not granted — identity worn like a coat tailored at last to fit.
